newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flexibility issue lurks behind routine GAC.
newsitem.headline: Flexibility issue lurks behind routine GAC.

text.p: European Union foreign ministers on Monday began their first meeting of 1997 with an agenda that officials said was uncomplicated and routine, but which could signal a turbulent year for the 15-nation bloc.

Lurking behind the formality of agreeing a common position on trade talks with Asian partners and smoothing over troubled relations with the United States was the issue of "flexibility", the future of an enlarged EU.
The flexibility issue is at the heart of attempts to rewrite the EU's treaties in order for the bloc to take in a number of applicant members from central and eastern Europe.
Formally known as the inter-governmental conference (IGC) the treaty talks are due to be completed during the six-month Dutch EU presidency and be formally agreed as the Treaty of Amsterdam.

"The very future of Europe is at stake in the next year if not the next few months," Spanish foreign minister Abel Matutes told the meeting. "If we are not able to succeed the very future of the EU is at stake."
But, with a British general election due before then, few EU diplomats believe they have enough time or political will to get the job done before June.
At the core of the reworking is flexibility, a method by which -- in extreme circumstances -- EU members can decide which new European agreements to embrace and which they can put off until later.
While most EU members favour some form of flexibility, they are divided over how to interpret it and whether nations "sitting out" a particular development should still have a say in how it proceeds.

Monday's meeting will first, however, address a range of routine issues ranging from establishing a common position for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the Europe-Asia Meeting (ASEN) forum next month.
Ministers will also discuss the situation in former Yugoslavia, the Great Lakes region and Belarus.
